prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms confined at a magic wavelength allow frequency measurements at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from B011 to B052, Katori and Ye as the sole part. The reason is not the count of supporters, which I do not treat as a scientific argument; it is that round 1 left my own case with a problem I cannot answer. I argued that B011 is the most original and least replaceable contribution, but the credit for aberration correction is split between the TEM lineage (Rose, Haider, Urban) and the STEM lineage (Krivanek, Dellby), and a three-name list cannot be written so that it is fair to both. Eriksson and Pearce each raised the Krivanek and Dellby point independently, and my own round-1 statement already conceded it rests on my recollection and not on the supplied evidence. A prize whose citation we would have to defend against a well-known omission is weaker than one with a defensible credit. On the physics, B052 holds up under the test I applied to B011, namely what the named people actually did and whether it can be said in one sentence: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength condition that cancels the light shift of the clock transition, Lamb-Dicke confinement in the lattice removes Doppler and recoil shifts, and Ye's group then showed what that buys, with many atoms interrogated in parallel and uncertainty near 1e-18. It has been reproduced by independent laboratories and species and is used in tests of relativity, searches for varying constants and clock comparisons. I think a citation tied to the magic-wavelength lattice scheme answers the chair's first question: the 2005 prize honoured the frequency comb and the 2012 prize honoured control of single ions, while the lattice scheme is a different physical solution that lets a large ensemble of neutral atoms be measured at once. I do not regard that as a mere accuracy improvement, but I accept that the wording must carry the distinction.
statement.case_against: The reservations I raised in round 1 have not disappeared. The overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is real, and whether the lattice clock is a distinct discovery or an increment on a lineage already honoured is a judgement, not a fact; it depends on the citation naming the magic-wavelength lattice and not clocks in general. The redefinition of the second has not happened, and I would not want the citation to lean on it. Credit is narrower than the history: PTB, SYRTE, NIST and Takamoto's group in Tokyo built or improved strontium and ytterbium platforms in parallel, and several members, like me, recall the priority details from memory. Against my own earlier position I should also say that B011 has not become a weaker piece of science; I still think aberration correction is an invention of exactly the kind the statutes describe, and I would be uneasy if the committee treated it as merely enabling methodology. Its problem is the credit boundary, and that is a reason to defer, not to dismiss.

responses.point: The lattice clock is a clean two-name credit that tests physics and not only serves as a tool, and the thorium-clock connection should be kept out of this citation.
responses.response: I agree on the thorium point and on keeping the citation to the lattice scheme. I accept the substance of his argument about confirmation: the clock has independent reproduction at several laboratories, and that is a firmer position than I can claim for a single credit line on B011. I still do not accept that an instrument is for that reason less of a discovery-or-invention achievement, since the clock is also an instrument and the line he draws is thinner than he suggests. But the distinction that matters to me now is attribution, and there the two-name credit is easier to defend. His disclosure about John Hall's laboratory seems to me a connection to note, and not a bar, given that no joint work with Katori or Ye is recorded.

responses.point: B011 maps cleanly onto Rose, Haider and Urban but the STEM correctors by Krivanek and Dellby were developed in parallel and weaken the attribution, so he would put it below the clocks.
responses.response: This is the point that moved me. I had treated the corrector as an object three people designed and made work, but he is right that the history has two lineages and a three-name list takes one. I would also hold him to the same standard for his own fallback, B010: if the credit for B011 is weakened by a missing parallel group, the Higgs credit is weakened more by thousands of colleagues. I would not agree that B011 belongs to a later year on its merits; I would say it needs a way of crediting both lineages, which the present list does not offer.

responses.point: He prefers B044 for its conceptual originality and a mature record, and asks whether analogue simulation has yet produced a decisive result, while ranking the clock seventh on overlap and timing.
responses.response: I take his originality argument seriously, and I share his worry about the overlap between the clock and the earlier prizes, which I raised myself. But his own account of B044 has an attribution problem I find at least as serious as the clock's: four names for three places, with Zoller also on B009 and Esslinger disputed. If the reservation about the clock is overlap and timing, I would ask him whether a citation limited to the magic-wavelength lattice would be acceptable to him, since the committee's question for him is whether the remaining objection is to the clock or to the ranking of his own candidate.

responses.point: He supports B011 in principle but notes the instrument-versus-discovery framing and the missing Krivanek and Dellby, and prefers B021 as common ground.
responses.response: I agree about the framing risk and have now acted on it. On B021 I do not move: the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is not only a fairness matter, since the HgTe experiment grew out of their proposal, so the citation cannot honestly credit the experiment without crediting that proposal. He offers a narrower citation limited to the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 invariant, and I would want to see that wording before I could regard it as defensible, but I do not think it avoids the issue. As he says himself, B052 is an acceptable fallback, and that is where I stand.

uncertainties: Whether the 2005 and 2012 overlaps can be answered in citation wording alone; I think so, but Mehlig and Eriksson have not yet said so.
Whether Katori and Ye is a sufficient credit given PTB, SYRTE, NIST and Takamoto; I rely on memory for the early priority details and so do others.
Whether the STEM and TEM lineages for B011 could be credited together in some later year; I have no evidence beyond my own recollection that they could not.
Whether my move reflects a changed scientific judgement or partly the weight of the other seven; I believe it is the attribution problem, but I cannot rule out the other.
statement.conflict_note: I am a transmission electron microscopist at Chalmers and I have worked with the technique in B011, which I ranked first in round 1; with my preference now on B052 that field proximity is no longer relevant to my preferred configuration, but the committee may wish to note that I defended B011 earlier. I have no documented connection to Katori, Ye, Rose, Haider or Urban, and no documented tie to the lattice clock community. Göran Johansson is also at Chalmers, and his preferred candidate B056 is not in my configuration.
